name: Nora Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play keyboard behind a community choir, teach three beginners and take little demo recording calls when they come. I am still learning to hold a group together when the singers rush. The good part is hearing shy people sing; the hard part is the hours spent travelling for a short paid rehearsal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that fit with home and the next few years?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner drives deliveries, and our children are grown and living elsewhere. We rent a flat, and we have less than a month of bills saved; my music fees are low and there are few similar posts nearby. I use AI every day to make a first practice schedule, but I correct it at the keyboard before anyone sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir a quicker rehearsal list is fine, but somebody still has to play along with the singers. I already use AI for a first timetable and check it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing radical changing would still leave my small fees and the rent due. One missed choir rehearsal could eat most of what we have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the choir, three pupils and paid demo calls, and ask the choir for next term’s dates and rehearsal fees in writing. In the first year of a plateau I would cut the paid music app I rarely use, and put one quarter of any cleared extra demo fee after rent, food and bus fares toward one month of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about ordinary work and rent, even without an AI shock. A thin envelope of savings makes a cancelled Tuesday loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Tuesday is cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the choir pays the agreed cancellation fee and tell my partner that evening. A date written in pencil cannot buy groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cut only one app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The free metronome does the bit I use. I will not cut the bus fare that gets me to paid pupils.

think: My **rent** is exposed to one missed paid rehearsal.
Our **sub-month reserve** leaves little room for ordinary cancellations.

Cancel **unused music app** and save a quarter of cleared extra demo fees after essentials toward one month.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent and irregular pay already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our choir that booking software may move faster than I do, but singers still need a keyboard in the room. I would ask who pays when a rehearsal is cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The demo callers could use generated tracks and the choir might trim paid planning hours. I would lose money I actually use for rent, and the delivery work at home is not guaranteed every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would get the choir’s paid dates and cancellation terms in writing, and keep three pupils. If two demo calls in a row disappear, I would apply for a posted paid library-events assistant vacancy only if my secondary education is accepted and its written net pay after bus fares replaces the lost fees; I would keep music work until I have a signed offer, and in the first year of disruption I would do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because those small recording fees are not spare money. I could find other work, but few music jobs are nearby and our savings would not cover a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a volunteer library shift first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would ask for paid hours and what the duties are. I cannot swap a paid keyboard hour for a promising badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the choir treasurer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the cancellation rule before I book the bus. A rehearsed song is not a fee if the room stays locked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2028 thinking AGI can make a demo track before a robot could sit at my keyboard around 2031. The choir should tell us about paid dates early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the little demo calls to stop and perhaps one choir night to be cut in 2028. That would take rent money, and less than a month saved is no buffer for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would ask for signed choir dates and keep my three pupils. In the first year after 2028, if demo orders stop and a choir night is cut, I would seek an advertised paid library-events job only if my secondary schooling qualifies and written net pay after the bus replaces the lost music fees; I would keep the remaining choir and pupils until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing two kinds of income quickly. I can fill out applications. I cannot make a paid library-events vacancy appear near the bus line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown children help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not build a plan around their money; they have bills of their own. I would tell them what is happening, not send an invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop playing while you look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Any paid choir night and pupil hour stays on my calendar until an actual replacement job starts.

I would ask the choir for **signed paid dates** early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that five years gives us a little time to make paid rehearsal plans. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and robot players around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Demos might disappear by 2031, but I can use the years to learn whether another small paid music line exists. I cannot afford a hall deposit on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep choir, pupils and demos, and ask the senior centre whether it would buy a separate monthly sing-along. I would start only with a signed paid order covering my playing and preparation, bus fare and any accompanist I hire; in the first year after 2031 I would repeat only while each order pays those costs, and keep the choir nights that still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about income over the next few years, though five years gives me time to ask a real buyer. I can try one senior-centre sing-along without putting rent money down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the centre room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The centre would provide its room under the order, or I would not book the date. I have no room money to risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring another player for free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the written fee has to include any accompanist’s rehearsal and performance time. I will play alone if the order pays only for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that 2036 thinking AGI and robot keyboard players around 2039 are not the same year. I would also tell the choir to put the fee on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I cannot assume I am still on the choir bench. A decade does not fill our savings by itself. We are already close to the rent each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid choir nights, pupils and demos, and save a quarter of cleared extra demo fees after rent, food and buses toward one month of bills. Over the decade I would seek signed senior-centre sing-along orders only when the centre provides the room and pays my playing/preparation, bus and any hired player; in the first year after 2036 I would repeat only with those paid terms and keep any choir work still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the rent is tight today, not only in 2036. More time helps me ask for paid orders, but it does not guarantee them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you promise to stop work at a certain birthday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not set a retirement date. I would look at our bills and the work I can actually do, not promise an income we do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the centre will not pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not run a free event and call it a new income. I would keep applying for paid local work while holding the choir dates I have.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture is worst because demos and a choir night could go before I can replace the rent money. Written paid dates, a real library vacancy and bus fares that still leave a net wage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens between a booking and the payment. I can be grateful for a room full of singers and still need the fee to clear before Friday rent.

headlineQuote: I can be grateful for a room full of singers and still need the fee to clear before Friday rent.
portrait: Nora is a **junior keyboard player** still learning, with secondary schooling and low music fees.
She has **less than one month** saved, a delivery-driving partner, grown children and rent to meet.
She uses **AI daily** for draft schedules but checks them at the keyboard.
She seeks **written pay** for choir, library work or a separate centre sing-along.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could remove demos and a choir night before rent money is replaced.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written paid dates**, a real library opening and net wages after bus fares.
